---
title: "One day, methods – the housing-audit case"
subtitle: "Four parts of ninety minutes, with a facilitator"
---
This is the one-day course on the housing-audit case with the methods in the foreground. It works on one field experiment, in which emails that differed only in the name that signed them were sent to public housing authorities in the United States, and on a claim of the original authors (OAs) that five analysts reanalysed for Multi100. Across the day you work as analyst no. 6. You write the estimand statement behind the claim and finish a causal graph of the experiment, and you reproduce one of the five reanalyses, whichever you choose. You then spend the afternoon on robustness. You work through a menu of defensible analyses, send the one that you would defend to the class chart, read the chart against the 64 specifications on the curve of the claim, and declare one analysis in a shortened preregistration template before you run it.

What you leave with is a report of your own, two marks on the class chart, one explored and one declared, and the place of your result on the curve.

## How you work

The day is taught mainly in the browser lab, a page of the course site on which R runs inside your browser, with nothing to install. Open it in a tab of its own and keep this page open beside it. Each part of the day has a page that lists its steps in order, and every step that you work at the keyboard has a button that opens the lab at the right task. If you have installed R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), the downloadable workspace holds the same tasks and gives the same numbers, and the setup page explains how to install it. The slides are on the [slides page](slides.qmd), and each part opens with a link to its place in the deck.

[Open the browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"} [Install R and the workspace](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

Several of the steps are things that the class does together, such as everyone typing the value that they have just reproduced and holding it back until the facilitator says go, so the day needs a facilitator. Some stretches of the slides are optional, a short tour of the toolchain and of R in the morning and a closer look at the statistics in the afternoon, and the facilitator switches them on or off to suit the class.

## The parts of the day

- **[Before the day](before.qmd)** (about an hour, more with the installation). You read the case study and open the browser lab once, and you install R, an IDE and the workspace if you want to work there.
- **[Part 1 – Credibility and tools](part-1.qmd)** (ninety minutes). The part asks what a claim is for and why the field talks of a crisis, sets out the evidence on reproduction, robustness and replication and the toolchain, and ends with R running on your machine.
- **[Part 2 – The claim and its estimand](part-2.qmd)** (ninety minutes, after a break of thirty minutes). You meet the paper and the five analysts, estimands and a short course on causal graphs, and then you write the estimand statement and finish the graph.
- **[Part 3 – Reproduction and exploration](part-3.qmd)** (ninety minutes, after an hour for lunch). You reproduce one of the five reanalyses, then work the specification menu and put an exploratory mark on the class chart.
- **[Part 4 – Multiverse, replication and preregistration](part-4.qmd)** (ninety minutes, after a break of thirty minutes). The class reads its chart against the curve of 64 and meets the replication with new data, and each participant declares one analysis, runs it and reports it.
- **[After the day](after.qmd)** (as long as you like). The page says where to go next in the companion curriculum.

[Start with Before the day](before.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
